{{Short description|Topological space that becomes totally disconnected with the removal of a single point}}
[[File:Kuratowski fan.svg|thumb|300px|The Knaster–Kuratowski fan]]

In [[topology]], a branch of mathematics, the '''Knaster&ndash;Kuratowski fan''' (named after Polish mathematicians [[Bronisław Knaster]] and [[Kazimierz Kuratowski]]) is a specific [[connected space|connected]] [[topological space]] with the property that the removal of a single point makes it [[totally disconnected]]. It is also known as '''Cantor's leaky tent'''{{sfn|Steen|Seebach|1995|loc=counterexampe 128}} (after [[Georg Cantor]]).

The same space with the [[apex (geometry)|apex]] point removed is called the '''punctured Knaster-Kuratowski fan''' or '''Cantor's [[teepee]]'''.{{sfn|Steen|Seebach|1995|loc=counterexample 129}}

==Construction==
To construct the fan start with the [[Cantor set]] which we will call <math>C</math> along the x axis and a point at <math>\left(\tfrac1{2},\tfrac1{2}\right)</math> which we will call <math>p</math>. Join every point in <math>C</math> to <math>p</math> with a straight line. We now have a set that is [[Connected space|connected]] and becomes disconnected if we remove <math>p</math>.

To make the set [[totally disconnected]] when we remove <math>p</math> we need to remove more points. If we look at how the Cantor set <math>C</math> was constructed we see that some points in <math>C</math> like <math>\tfrac1{3}</math> or 1 were the endpoints of [[Interval (mathematics)|intervals]] we removed when constructing it and others like <math>\tfrac1{4}</math> are not. We use this to decide which of the points we remove from every line. If the point at the bottom of a line (which will be part of <math>C</math>) is one of the points that was an end point of an interval we remove all coordinates with [[irrational number|irrational]] y coordinates. Otherwise we remove all points on the line with [[rational number|rational]] y coordinates. This set is the Knaster–Kuratowski fan.

==Properties==

The fan  is [[connected space|connected]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Arthur Steen |first1=lyyn |title=Counterexamples in Topology |publisher=Courier Corporation, 2013 |isbn=9780486319292 |page=145 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gc3DAgAAQBAJ&dq=cantor%27s+leaky+tent&pg=PA145}}</ref> but becomes [[totally disconnected]] if we remove <math>p</math>.

The proof of connectedness (that you cannot divide the fan into 2 [[open set|open]] [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] sets) is not trivial but can be thought of as starting with <math>p</math> in one of the sets and then having to add a little region around <math>p</math> to make the set open. You then need to add a little region around each of the points you added making the set slightly bigger. This continues until the whole fan is in the set<ref name=":01">{{cite web |title=A Few of My Favorite Spaces: Cantor's Leaky Tent |website=[[Scientific American]] |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/blog/roots-of-unity/a-few-of-my-favorite-spaces-cantor-s-leaky-tent/ |access-date=30 October 2025}}</ref>

To show that the fan is totally disconnected when you remove <math>p</math> you can start by noticing that each of the lines is now disconnected and then carry on splitting each of the lines down until you are left with individual points.<ref name=":01" />
